bookSections.title: Find and Use the Position-to-Term Rule

preamble.whatYouWillLearn: You will use position-to-term rules to find any term in a sequence, like the 50th, without listing them all, and work forwards and backwards through function machines. You will also find terms in special sequences: square numbers, cube numbers, and matchstick and tile patterns.
preamble.whyItMatters: Spotting a pattern lets you predict what comes next instead of counting one by one. Position-to-term rules and letters for unknown numbers are the start of algebra, which you will use a lot in secondary school. Patterns also train you to explain why a rule works.
realWorld: Rows of seats in a stadium that grow by the same number each row: how many seats in row 30?
Saving RM 5 more each week in a savings jar
Floor tiles laid in growing square patterns
Stacking cubes into bigger and bigger cubes: 1, 8, 27, 64 ...
A taxi fare rule: a fixed charge plus an amount for every kilometre

subtopics.title: Position-to-term rules
subtopics.summary: Use a rule like term = 4 x position + 1 to find any term, and work backwards to test whether a number is in a sequence.

subtopics.title: Function machines and letters
subtopics.summary: Find outputs and inputs of function machines, and use letters for unknown numbers in addition and subtraction.

subtopics.title: Square, cube and spatial patterns
subtopics.summary: Use square and cube numbers to make sequences, and find rules for matchstick and tile patterns.

subtopics.title: Square numbers and cube numbers
subtopics.summary: Recognise square numbers such as 7^2 = 49 (7^2 means 7 x 7) and cube numbers from 1 to 125 such as 4^3 = 64 (4^3 means 4 x 4 x 4).

questions.prompt: The position-to-term rule for a sequence is: term = 3 x position. What is the 5th term?
questions.solution: Put the position, 5, into the rule: term = 3 x 5 = 15.

misconceptions.0: You added 3 and 5. The rule says multiply: 3 x 5 = 15.
misconceptions.1: You wrote 3 and 5 side by side. The rule says multiply the position by 3: 3 x 5 = 15.
misconceptions.2: You used position 6. The 5th term uses position 5: 3 x 5 = 15.

questions.prompt: The position-to-term rule for a sequence is: term = 2 x position + 1. What is the 10th term?
questions.solution: Put 10 into the rule. Multiply first: 2 x 10 = 20. Then add 1: 20 + 1 = 21.

misconceptions.0: You added 1 to the position first (2 x 11 = 22). Multiply first, then add: 2 x 10 = 20, 20 + 1 = 21.
misconceptions.2: You added all the numbers: 2 + 10 + 1. The rule says multiply the position by 2 first.
misconceptions.3: You did 2 x 10 = 20 but forgot the '+ 1' at the end of the rule.

questions.prompt: True or false: The sequence 5, 10, 15, 20, ... has the position-to-term rule: term = position + 5.
questions.solution: Test the rule. Position 1: 1 + 5 = 6, but the 1st term is 5. So the rule is wrong. The correct rule is term = 5 x position (5 x 1 = 5, 5 x 2 = 10, 5 x 3 = 15).

misconceptions.common: Seeing 'goes up by 5' and writing '+ 5'. When a sequence goes up in steps of 5, the position-to-term rule starts with 5 x position.

questions.prompt: Match each position-to-term rule to the first four terms of the sequence it makes.
questions.solution: Put positions 1, 2, 3, 4 into each rule. 2 x position: 2, 4, 6, 8. 2 x position + 3: 5, 7, 9, 11. 3 x position - 1: 2, 5, 8, 11. The sequence 3, 5, 7, 9 (rule 2 x position + 1) is not used.

misconceptions.common: Looking only at the step. Two sequences go up in 2s, so also check the first term: 2 x 1 + 3 = 5.

questions.prompt: Look at the sequence 4, 7, 10, 13, ... Which is its position-to-term rule?
questions.solution: The step is 3, so start with 3 x position: 3, 6, 9, 12. Each term is 1 more than these, so term = 3 x position + 1. Check: 3 x 4 + 1 = 13.

misconceptions.1: 'Add 3' is the term-to-term rule. As a position-to-term rule, position + 3 gives 4, 5, 6, ... A step of 3 means 3 x position.
misconceptions.2: This gives 3, 6, 9, 12, which is 1 less than every term. You need to add 1.
misconceptions.3: This gives 7, 10, 13, ... and starts one term too late. Test position 1: 3 x 1 + 4 = 7, not 4.

questions.prompt: A sequence starts 6, 11, 16, 21, ... What is the 20th term?
questions.solution: The step is 5, so compare with 5 x position: 5, 10, 15, 20. Each term is 1 more, so term = 5 x position + 1. The 20th term is 5 x 20 + 1 = 100 + 1 = 101.

misconceptions.common: Adding 20 steps of 5 to the first term (6 + 100 = 106). From the 1st term to the 20th term there are only 19 steps: 6 + 19 x 5 = 101. Another slip is forgetting the + 1 and answering 100.

questions.prompt: A sequence has the rule term = 4 x position + 3, so it starts 7, 11, 15, 19, ... Which of these numbers is in the sequence?
questions.solution: Undo the rule: subtract 3, then divide by 4. If you get a whole number, that is the position. 75 - 3 = 72 and 72 ÷ 4 = 18. So 75 is the 18th term. Check: 4 x 18 + 3 = 75.

misconceptions.0: 72 is a multiple of 4, but every term is a multiple of 4 plus 3. 72 - 3 = 69, which is not a multiple of 4.
misconceptions.1: 77 ends in 7 like the first term, but that does not make it a term. 77 - 3 = 74, and 74 ÷ 4 = 18.5, which is not a whole number.
misconceptions.3: Every term is odd, but not every odd number is a term. 81 - 3 = 78, and 78 ÷ 4 = 19.5, which is not a whole number.

questions.skill: testing if a number is in a sequence

questions.prompt: The rule for a sequence is term = 5 x position - 2. Which position has the term 48?
questions.solution: Work backwards using inverse operations. Undo '- 2': 48 + 2 = 50. Undo 'x 5': 50 ÷ 5 = 10. Check: 5 x 10 - 2 = 48.

misconceptions.0: You took away 2 and then divided by 5. To undo '- 2' you must add 2: 48 + 2 = 50, and 50 ÷ 5 = 10.
misconceptions.2: You put 48 into the rule as if it were a position (5 x 48 - 2). 48 is a term, so work backwards to find its position.
misconceptions.3: You added 2 to undo the '- 2', but forgot to undo the 'x 5'. 50 ÷ 5 = 10.

questions.skill: testing if a number is in a sequence

questions.prompt: In a school hall, Row 1 has 12 chairs. Each row has 3 more chairs than the row in front of it. How many chairs are in Row 25?
questions.solution: From Row 1 to Row 25 there are 24 steps of 3. 24 x 3 = 72. So Row 25 has 12 + 72 = 84 chairs. (As a rule: chairs = 3 x row number + 9. Check Row 1: 3 + 9 = 12.)

misconceptions.common: Adding 25 steps of 3 (12 + 75 = 87). Row 1 already has its 12 chairs, so there are only 24 jumps to get to Row 25.

questions.prompt: True or false: The number 100 is a term in the sequence with the rule term = 6 x position - 4.
questions.solution: Undo the rule: 100 + 4 = 104, and 104 ÷ 6 = 17 remainder 2, which is not a whole number. The 17th term is 6 x 17 - 4 = 98 and the 18th is 6 x 18 - 4 = 104, so the sequence jumps over 100. False.

misconceptions.common: Thinking 100 is a term because all the terms are even. Every term is 4 less than a multiple of 6, and 100 + 4 = 104 is not a multiple of 6.

questions.skill: testing if a number is in a sequence

questions.prompt: A sequence starts 3, 7, 11, 15, ... Omar says, 'The 50th term is 200, because 50 x 4 = 200.' What is the 50th term?
questions.solution: The step is 4, so compare with 4 x position: 4, 8, 12, 16. Each term is 1 less, so term = 4 x position - 1. The 50th term is 4 x 50 - 1 = 199. Omar forgot the '- 1'.

misconceptions.0: This is Omar's mistake. 4 x position gives 4, 8, 12, ..., but the 1st term is 3, so every term is 1 less: 4 x 50 - 1 = 199.
misconceptions.1: You started at 3 and added 50 steps of 4. From the 1st term to the 50th term there are only 49 steps: 3 + 49 x 4 = 199.
misconceptions.2: You worked out 49 x 4 = 196 but forgot to add the first term, 3.

questions.prompt: What is the next number in this sequence of square numbers? 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...
questions.solution: The square numbers are 1 x 1, 2 x 2, 3 x 3, 4 x 4, 5 x 5. The next one is 6 x 6 = 36.

misconceptions.0: You added 9 again. The gaps grow by 2 each time (3, 5, 7, 9), so the next gap is 11: 25 + 11 = 36.
misconceptions.1: You did 6 x 2. A square number is a number times itself: 6 x 6 = 36.
misconceptions.2: 49 = 7 x 7 is a square number, but you skipped 6 x 6 = 36.

questions.prompt: The sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, ... has the rule term = position x position. What is the 12th term?
questions.solution: Put position 12 into the rule: 12 x 12 = 144.

misconceptions.0: 12 x 2 = 24 is doubling. Square numbers multiply the position by itself: 12 x 12 = 144.
misconceptions.2: 121 = 11 x 11 is the 11th term. The 12th term is 12 x 12 = 144.
misconceptions.3: 1728 = 12 x 12 x 12 is a cube number. The rule only multiplies twice: 12 x 12 = 144.

questions.prompt: True or false: The cube numbers start 1, 8, 27, 64, ...

misconceptions.common: Thinking '2 cubed' means 2 x 3 = 6. Cubing means multiplying the number by itself three times: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows Pattern 3 of a matchstick pattern. Each side of a small triangle is one matchstick. Pattern 1 is one triangle made from 3 matchsticks. To make each new pattern, you join one more triangle onto the end, sharing a side, which uses 2 more matchsticks. How many matchsticks are in Pattern 4?

diagram.caption: Pattern 3
diagram.alt: Pattern 3: three matchstick triangles in a row, pointing up, down and up, each sharing a side with the next.

questions.solution: Count the matchsticks in Pattern 3 in the diagram: 3 + 2 + 2 = 7. Pattern 4 joins one more triangle, which needs 2 more matchsticks: 7 + 2 = 9. (The patterns go 3, 5, 7, 9.)

misconceptions.0: You counted 3 sticks for every triangle. The triangles share sides, so each new one needs only 2 more sticks.
misconceptions.1: You did 4 x 2 = 8. Pattern 1 needs 3 sticks, not 2, so the total is 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 9.
misconceptions.3: 11 is Pattern 5. The patterns go 3, 5, 7, 9, so Pattern 4 has 9.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows Pattern 3 of a tile pattern. Pattern 1 is 1 tile. Pattern 2 is a square 2 tiles by 2 tiles. Pattern 3 is a square 3 tiles by 3 tiles, and so on. How many tiles are in Pattern 9?

diagram.caption: Pattern 3
diagram.alt: Pattern 3: a square of tiles, 3 tiles by 3 tiles.

questions.solution: Pattern 3 in the diagram is a 3 by 3 square: 3 x 3 = 9 tiles. Pattern n is an n by n square, so it has n x n tiles (a square number). Pattern 9 has 9 x 9 = 81 tiles.

misconceptions.1: You did 9 x 2. Pattern 9 is a 9 by 9 square, so it has 9 x 9 = 81 tiles.
misconceptions.2: You did 9 x 3. A 9 by 9 square has 9 rows of 9 tiles: 9 x 9 = 81.
misconceptions.3: 64 = 8 x 8 is Pattern 8. Pattern 9 is 9 x 9 = 81.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the numbers that are in the sequence of cube numbers 1, 8, 27, ...
questions.solution: 64 = 4 x 4 x 4, 125 = 5 x 5 x 5 and 1000 = 10 x 10 x 10 are cube numbers. 100, 9 and 16 are square numbers, not cube numbers.

misconceptions.1: 100 = 10 x 10 is a square number. 10 cubed is 10 x 10 x 10 = 1000.
misconceptions.3: 9 = 3 x 3 is a square number. 3 cubed is 3 x 3 x 3 = 27.
misconceptions.5: 16 = 4 x 4 is a square number. 4 cubed is 4 x 4 x 4 = 64.

questions.prompt: Work out the value of each, then put them in order from smallest to largest.

misconceptions.common: Thinking 3^3 means 3 x 3 = 9 or 3 + 3 + 3 = 9. 3^3 = 3 x 3 x 3 = 27, which is bigger than 5^2 = 25.

questions.prompt: Squares are made from matchsticks in a row. Each side of a small square is one matchstick. The diagram shows Pattern 3. Pattern 1 is 1 square made from 4 matchsticks. Each new pattern joins one more square onto the end of the row, sharing a side, so it uses 3 more matchsticks. How many matchsticks are in Pattern 10?

diagram.caption: Pattern 3
diagram.alt: Pattern 3: three matchstick squares in a row, each sharing a side with the next.

questions.solution: Pattern 3 in the diagram has 10 matchsticks (4 + 3 + 3). The patterns go 4, 7, 10, 13, ... The step is 3, so compare with 3 x pattern number: 3, 6, 9, 12. Each is 1 more, so matchsticks = 3 x pattern number + 1. Pattern 10: 3 x 10 + 1 = 31. (Or: 4 + 9 x 3 = 31.)

misconceptions.common: Doing 4 x 10 = 40. That counts every shared side twice; each new square needs only 3 new matchsticks.

questions.prompt: The sequence 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, ... is made by adding 1 to each square number (1 + 1, 4 + 1, 9 + 1, ...). Which position in the sequence has the term 145?
questions.solution: Take away the 1 that was added: 145 - 1 = 144. 144 = 12 x 12, so 144 is the 12th square number. That means 145 is the 12th term. Check: 12 x 12 + 1 = 145.

misconceptions.common: Answering 144 (that is a square number, not a position) or forgetting to take away the 1 first. Subtract 1, then find which number times itself makes 144.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows Pattern 4 of a tile pattern. Pattern 1 is a 1 by 1 square of tiles, Pattern 2 is a 2 by 2 square, Pattern 3 is a 3 by 3 square, and so on. How many more tiles does Pattern 8 have than Pattern 7?

diagram.caption: Pattern 4
diagram.alt: Pattern 4: a square of tiles, 4 tiles by 4 tiles.

questions.solution: Pattern 4 in the diagram is a 4 by 4 square of 16 tiles, so Pattern n has n x n tiles. Pattern 8 has 8 x 8 = 64 tiles. Pattern 7 has 7 x 7 = 49 tiles. The difference is 64 - 49 = 15.

misconceptions.0: You added just one row of 8. To grow a 7 by 7 square into an 8 by 8 square you add a row AND a column: 8 + 7 = 15.
misconceptions.2: You added a row of 8 and a column of 8, but the corner tile was counted twice. 8 + 8 - 1 = 15.
misconceptions.3: 64 is the total number of tiles in Pattern 8. The question asks how many MORE than Pattern 7: 64 - 49 = 15.

questions.prompt: True or false: The gaps between the square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, ... are the odd numbers 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, ...
questions.solution: 4 - 1 = 3, 9 - 4 = 5, 16 - 9 = 7, 25 - 16 = 9, 36 - 25 = 11. The gaps are the odd numbers, each 2 more than the last. True! (To grow one square into the next you add a row and a column, which always makes an odd number of tiles.)

misconceptions.common: Thinking the gaps between square numbers are all the same. For square numbers each gap is 2 more than the one before.

questions.prompt: Look at the function machine. The input is 5. What is the output?
questions.solution: Do the steps in order. First 5 x 4 = 20. Then 20 + 3 = 23.

misconceptions.1: You did the steps in the wrong order: (5 + 3) x 4 = 32. Follow the machine in order: 5 x 4 = 20, then 20 + 3 = 23.
misconceptions.3: You joined the 4 and the 3 into 'x 7': 5 x 7 = 35. Do one step at a time.

questions.prompt: A function machine subtracts 6. The output is 14. What was the input?
questions.solution: Work backwards with the inverse. The machine subtracts 6, so add 6: 14 + 6 = 20. Check: 20 - 6 = 14.

misconceptions.common: Subtracting 6 again (14 - 6 = 8). To go backwards through a machine, do the opposite operation: add 6.

questions.prompt: A function machine changes 3 into 12, 5 into 20 and 8 into 32. It does one operation. What is it? Write your answer like 'add 2' or 'multiply by 2'.
questions.solution: Test 'multiply by 4' on every pair: 3 x 4 = 12, 5 x 4 = 20, 8 x 4 = 32. It works every time.

misconceptions.common: Answering 'add 9'. It works for 3 into 12, but 5 + 9 = 14, not 20. A rule must work for every pair.

questions.prompt: True or false: If a + 15 = 42, then a = 27.
questions.solution: Use the inverse: a = 42 - 15 = 27. Check: 27 + 15 = 42. True!

misconceptions.common: Adding 15 instead of subtracting it (42 + 15 = 57). To find a, undo the '+ 15' by subtracting 15.

questions.prompt: a and b are two whole numbers. a + b = 20, and a is 6 more than b. What is a?
questions.solution: Think of two bars: b, and a = b + 6. Take away the extra 6: 20 - 6 = 14. Share 14 between the two equal bars: b = 7. Then a = 7 + 6 = 13. Check: 13 + 7 = 20 and 13 - 7 = 6.

misconceptions.0: You worked out 20 - 6 = 14 and stopped. 14 is two equal parts (b + b), so b = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 and a = 7 + 6 = 13.
misconceptions.1: 7 is b, the smaller number. a is 6 more: 7 + 6 = 13.
misconceptions.2: You halved 20. That would make a and b equal, but a must be 6 more than b.

questions.prompt: Look at the function machine. The output is 31. What was the input?
questions.solution: Work backwards, undoing the steps in reverse order. Undo '- 5': 31 + 5 = 36. Undo 'x 3': 36 ÷ 3 = 12. Check: 12 x 3 = 36, 36 - 5 = 31.

misconceptions.common: Undoing the steps in the wrong order (dividing 31 by 3 first) or using the same operations instead of the inverses. Undo the LAST step first.

questions.prompt: Look at the function machine. Match each input to its output.

misconceptions.common: Doing + 7 before ÷ 2 (10 + 7 = 17, 17 ÷ 2 = 8.5). Follow the steps in the order the machine does them.

questions.prompt: A function machine turns 2 into 5, 3 into 7 and 6 into 13. Which rule works for ALL three?
questions.solution: Test each rule on all three pairs. x 2, then + 1: 2 x 2 + 1 = 5, 3 x 2 + 1 = 7, 6 x 2 + 1 = 13. It works every time.

misconceptions.0: '+ 3' works for 2 into 5, but 3 + 3 = 6, not 7. A rule must work for every pair.
misconceptions.1: This works for 2 into 5, but 3 x 3 - 1 = 8, not 7.
misconceptions.3: This works for 3 into 7, but 2 + 4 = 6, not 5.

questions.prompt: Look at the function machine. The output is 9. What was the input?
questions.solution: Work backwards. Undo '+ 2.5': 9 - 2.5 = 6.5. Multiplying by 0.5 halves a number, so undo it by doubling: 6.5 x 2 = 13. Check: 13 x 0.5 = 6.5, 6.5 + 2.5 = 9.

misconceptions.common: Undoing 'x 0.5' by multiplying by 0.5 again (6.5 x 0.5 = 3.25). Multiplying by 0.5 is the same as halving, so the inverse is doubling.

questions.prompt: a and b are positive whole numbers (1, 2, 3, ...). a + b = 12 and a is greater than b. Select ALL the values that a could be.
questions.solution: List the pairs that add to 12 with a bigger than b and b at least 1: a = 7, b = 5; a = 8, b = 4; a = 9, b = 3; a = 10, b = 2; a = 11, b = 1. From the list, a could be 7, 9 or 11.

misconceptions.0: If a = 5 then b = 7, so a would be smaller than b.
misconceptions.1: If a = 6 then b = 6. a must be greater than b, not equal to it.
misconceptions.5: If a = 12 then b = 0, but b must be a positive whole number (1 or more).

questions.prompt: Wei Ming is w years old. His sister Mei Lin is 4 years younger than him. Which expression gives Mei Lin's age in 5 years' time?
questions.solution: Mei Lin's age now is w - 4. In 5 years she will be w - 4 + 5 = w + 1. Check with a number: if Wei Ming is 10, Mei Lin is 6 now and 11 in 5 years, and 10 + 1 = 11.

misconceptions.1: You subtracted both numbers (w - 4 - 5). In 5 years Mei Lin will be OLDER, so add the 5: w - 4 + 5 = w + 1.
misconceptions.2: You added both numbers. Mei Lin is 4 years YOUNGER, so subtract 4 and then add 5: w - 4 + 5 = w + 1.
misconceptions.3: That is Mei Lin's age now. In 5 years she will be 5 years older: w - 4 + 5 = w + 1.

questions.prompt: What is 7^2?
questions.solution: 7^2 means 7 squared, which is 7 x 7 = 49.

misconceptions.1: This works out 7 x 2. 7^2 means 7 x 7.
misconceptions.2: This writes 7 twice. 7^2 means 7 multiplied by itself.
misconceptions.3: 343 is 7^3 = 7 x 7 x 7. 7^2 uses only two 7s.

questions.prompt: What is 4^3?
questions.solution: 4^3 means 4 cubed: 4 x 4 x 4. 4 x 4 = 16, then 16 x 4 = 64.

misconceptions.common: Answering 12 by working out 4 x 3. 4^3 means 4 x 4 x 4.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a cube number?
questions.solution: Cube numbers are 1 x 1 x 1 = 1, 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, 3 x 3 x 3 = 27, 4 x 4 x 4 = 64, 5 x 5 x 5 = 125. 27 is in the list.

misconceptions.0: 9 = 3 x 3, so it is a SQUARE number, not a cube number.
misconceptions.1: 6 = 2 x 3. A cube number is a number times itself three times, e.g. 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.
misconceptions.3: 16 = 4 x 4, a square number. It is not 1, 8, 27, 64 or 125.

questions.prompt: What is the special name for the numbers 1, 8, 27, 64 and 125?
questions.solution: 1 = 1 x 1 x 1, 8 = 2 x 2 x 2, 27 = 3 x 3 x 3, 64 = 4 x 4 x 4, 125 = 5 x 5 x 5. They are cube numbers, because a cube of small blocks that is 2 long, 2 wide and 2 high has 8 blocks.

misconceptions.common: Saying square numbers. Square numbers come from 2 equal numbers multiplied (like 3 x 3 = 9); these come from 3 equal numbers multiplied.

questions.prompt: Work out each value, then put them in order from smallest to largest.

misconceptions.common: Treating the small number as 'times', e.g. 3^3 = 9 or 2^3 = 6. The small number tells you how many times to multiply the number by itself.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the square numbers.
questions.solution: Square numbers: 6 x 6 = 36, 8 x 8 = 64, 10 x 10 = 100. 48, 90 and 125 are not the result of a whole number multiplied by itself.

misconceptions.1: 48 is between 6 x 6 = 36 and 7 x 7 = 49, so it is not a square number.
misconceptions.3: 90 is between 9 x 9 = 81 and 10 x 10 = 100, so it is not a square number.
misconceptions.5: 125 = 5 x 5 x 5 is a CUBE number. It is between 11 x 11 = 121 and 12 x 12 = 144, so it is not a square number.

questions.prompt: A square garden has an area of 121 m^2. How long is one side of the garden?
questions.solution: Area of a square = side x side. Which number times itself is 121? 11 x 11 = 121. So each side is 11 m.

misconceptions.0: This halves the area. For a square, you need the number that multiplied by ITSELF gives 121.
misconceptions.2: This divides 121 by 4, which you would do with a perimeter, not an area.

questions.prompt: Work out 6^2 + 2^3.

misconceptions.0: This works out 6 x 2 = 12 and 2 x 3 = 6, then 12 + 6. The powers mean 6 x 6 and 2 x 2 x 2.
misconceptions.1: 6^2 = 36 is right, but 2^3 is 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, not 2 x 3 = 6.
misconceptions.2: This multiplies 36 x 8. The sign is +, so add: 36 + 8.

questions.prompt: True or false: 2^3 is the same as 3^2.
questions.solution: 2^3 = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8. 3^2 = 3 x 3 = 9. 8 is not the same as 9, so the statement is false.

misconceptions.common: Thinking the order does not matter because both use a 2 and a 3. 2^3 means three 2s multiplied; 3^2 means two 3s multiplied.

questions.prompt: Which number is BOTH a square number and a cube number?
questions.solution: 64 = 8 x 8, so it is a square number. 64 = 4 x 4 x 4, so it is also a cube number. It is both!

misconceptions.0: 8 = 2 x 2 x 2 is a cube number, but no whole number times itself makes 8 (2 x 2 = 4, 3 x 3 = 9).
misconceptions.1: 16 = 4 x 4 is a square number, but it is not a cube number (2 x 2 x 2 = 8, 3 x 3 x 3 = 27).
misconceptions.3: 27 = 3 x 3 x 3 is a cube number, but it is not a square number (5 x 5 = 25, 6 x 6 = 36).

questions.prompt: Daniel builds the large cube in the diagram from small 1 cm cubes. It is 5 small cubes long, 5 wide and 5 high. He then takes away a block of small cubes that is 3 long, 3 wide and 3 high from one corner. How many small cubes are left?
questions.solution: The large cube has 5 x 5 x 5 = 125 small cubes. The block taken away has 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 small cubes. 125 - 27 = 98 small cubes are left.

misconceptions.common: Answering 116 by taking away 3 x 3 = 9 instead of 3 x 3 x 3 = 27. The block that is removed is a cube too, so it has 3^3 = 27 small cubes.

questions.prompt: How many square numbers are there between 50 and 150?
questions.solution: 7 x 7 = 49 is too small. Then 8 x 8 = 64, 9 x 9 = 81, 10 x 10 = 100, 11 x 11 = 121, 12 x 12 = 144. 13 x 13 = 169 is too big. That is 5 square numbers.

misconceptions.common: Missing 144 (12 x 12) or 121 (11 x 11) because they are past the 10 times table.
